title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
hook: night six: in Bengal the drums start, and the goddess is welcomed as a married daughter coming home with her children

segments.voice: Yesterday was night five of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: Skandamata, a mother with her child, and a staircase of dolls. Whom did you call on? Day one thousand one hundred fourteen.

Drums. Big ones, slung on the shoulder, beaten with two sticks, and the sound carries down the lane. In Kolkata and across Bengal, around this point in the nights, Durga Puja gets under way. Inside a decorated tent called a pandal stands a clay goddess with many arms, a lion at her feet and the buffalo demon under her spear. But look at who's with her. Lakshmi on one side, Saraswati on the other. Ganesha. Kartikeya on his peacock. She hasn't come alone. She's brought the children. Tonight is the sixth name in the Kavacha's list, Katyayani, and in Bengal, a homecoming.
screen: `DRUMS DOWN THE LANE.` → `A GODDESS WITH HER CHILDREN.` → `SIXTH NIGHT: KATYAYANI.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Katyayani is the sixth in the Kavacha's list, and there's a story people tell about it: that she appeared in the hermitage of a sage called Katyayana, and took his name the way a daughter takes her father's. In the stories of the nine forms, she's the warrior form, the one who goes out to meet the buffalo demon. Now Bengal. In Bengal the goddess has another name, Uma, and another story wrapped around the battle. Uma is the daughter of the mountain king, Himalaya, married far away to Shiva on Mount Kailash. Once a year, the songs say, she comes home to her parents' house for a few days, and brings her children with her. Her mother has been waiting at the door all year. There are Bengali songs, called agamani songs, sung in the mother's voice: is my Uma coming? Is she thin? Is her husband treating her well? So the same festival holds two pictures at once. On the altar, the goddess with many arms, killing a demon. In the songs, a married daughter on a visit, and a mother who can't stop fussing over her. Neither picture cancels the other. That's the sixth lesson of the curriculum. The goddess who protects the universe is also somebody's child, coming home. And the homecoming has an end. When the festival is over, she leaves, and the leaving is part of it. People say goodbye to her the way you'd say goodbye to a daughter at the station.
screen: `KATYAYANI, THE SIXTH NAME.` · `UMA, DAUGHTER OF THE MOUNTAIN.` · `A MOTHER WAITING AT THE DOOR.` · `WARRIOR AND DAUGHTER AT ONCE.` · then, large: `SHE IS COMING HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: wait at the door for someone. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone you love who lives far away, or whom you don't see often enough: a child grown and gone, a parent, a sibling, an old friend. Picture them walking up to your door. Let yourself be the mother in the songs for a minute. Are they eating? Are they all right? Then let the worry soften into welcome. Just be glad they exist. If you pray, you can hold them before the goddess, or before God, in whatever words you use. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Night six: Katyayani in the Kavacha's list, and in Bengal, Uma coming home to her mother with her children.
Your line: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Today, send one message to someone far away that asks only: are you eating, are you well? Day one thousand one hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: In Bengal, Durga Puja centers on clay images of Durga with Lakshmi, Saraswati, Ganesha and Kartikeya in pandals, and songs welcome her as Uma, a daughter visiting her parents; where the nine forms are kept, the sixth night honors Katyayani.

fork.setup: you're Uma's mother. your daughter married far away, and she's coming home for a few days. what's on your mind as you wait?
options: whether she's well, and eating, and treated kindly.
fork.reveal: the agamani songs fuss like a mother: is she thin? is her husband good to her? the goddess of the universe is somebody's daughter.

original.note: Sanskrit: Katyayani, the sixth of the nine forms named in the Devi Kavacha.

trapdoor: what you thought: Durga Puja is just Durga killing a demon.
what it means: the battle is on the altar, but the songs tell of a daughter coming home to her parents, with her children.
what a scholar hears: agamani songs, a Bengali genre sung in the mother's voice, welcoming Uma from Kailash; her leaving at the end is mourned.
